title: Doom
shortDescription: John Carmack and John Romero's visceral sci-fi hellscape that popularized texture-mapped 3D rendering, networked deathmatches, and shareware distribution.
historicalSignificance: Revolutionized 3D computer graphics, defined the first-person shooter genre, inaugurated multiplayer LAN deathmatch culture, and pioneered user modding ecosystems via WAD files.

editorialContent.overview: Uploaded to university FTP servers in the early hours of December 10, 1993, by Texas independent developer id Software, Doom unleashed an unprecedented technological and cultural shockwave across computing. Melding industrial heavy-metal aesthetics with frenetic arcade speed and demonic horror, Doom established the first-person shooter as the preeminent technological showcase of personal computing.
editorialContent.gameplayMechanics: Players step into the combat boots of an unnamed space marine stranded on Phobos and Deimos after an interdimensional portal disaster. Combat emphasizes aggressive spatial positioning, circle-strafing, and rapid weapon cycling between shotguns, the rocket launcher, the plasma rifle, and the devastating BFG 9000. Enemies boast distinct behaviors, infighting mechanics when accidentally hit by peer crossfire, and aggressive sensory line-of-sight tracking.
editorialContent.technicalInnovation: Conceived and programmed by John Carmack in C on NeXTSTEP workstations and compiled for x86 via DOS4GW protected-mode extenders, the Doom engine rendered non-orthogonal textured walls, fluctuating ceiling heights, and dynamic sector lighting. Carmack employed Binary Space Partitioning (BSP) trees to pre-sort static 2.5D world geometry, allowing standard 386 and 486 PCs to render complex texture-mapped environments at high framerates in 320 × 200 VGA Mode 13h.
editorialContent.culturalImpact: Distributed primarily as a freely distributable five-episode shareware release, Doom was installed on an estimated ten million personal computers within two years, famously prompting corporate and university IT departments to ban the game due to clogged local area networks. Its modular WAD file architecture catalyzed modern video game modding, serving as the training ground for hundreds of future industry leaders.
editorialContent.preservationNotes: Preserved through original floppy disk shareware releases (v1.0 to v1.9) and the open-sourcing of the Doom source code in 1997. Authentic preservation emphasizes software-rendered column drawing without modern OpenGL filtering, accurate 35 Hz engine tick timing, and OPL2/OPL3 FM sound synthesis.

sourceReferences: Kushner, David. 'Masters of Doom: How Two Guys Created an Empire and Transformed Pop Culture', Random House (2003)
Carmack, John. 'Doom Engine Architecture and BSP Trees', id Software Technical Notes (1994)
Romero, John. 'Doom Guy: Life in First Person', Abrams Press (2023)
